data: These pre-training objectives teach language models syntax, semantics, and context by predicting corrupted, omitted, or shifted parts of text.
data.autoregressive--prefix-models#Autoregres: Causal LM (Causal Language Modeling): Predicts the next token strictly from left to right using directional masking (standard GPT architecture). Each token only attends to preceding tokens. Prefix LM: Allows full bidirectional attention over an initial prompt (“prefix”), then switches to standard autoregressive causal generation to predict the continuation (e.g., T5 decoder/prefix mode).
data.masking--denoising-objectives#Masking \u: Masked LM (MLM): Masks random tokens with a special tag (e.g., [MASK]) and trains the model to predict the original hidden words using bidirectional context (BERT-style). BERT-style MLM: An implementation detail of MLM where masked positions are replaced 80% of the time with [MASK], 10% with a random token, and 10% kept unchanged, forcing the model to evaluate all token representations. MASS-style (Masked Sequence to Sequence): Masks a contiguous span of tokens in the encoder, and uses the decoder to autoregressively reconstruct only the masked segment. Span Masking: Instead of masking individual words at random, masks contiguous sequences of tokens (spans) to make recovery harder and force deeper context comprehension (e.g., SpanBERT). Sentinel Masking (Span Corruption): Replaces entire masked spans with unique sentinel tokens (e.g., , ), training the decoder to output only the sentinels followed by their missing spans (used by T5).
data.sentence--document-level-objectives#Sent: Next Sentence Prediction (NSP): Feeds two sentences and predicts whether the second sentence logically follows the first in the original text (BERT pre-training). Sentence Comparison: Computes sentence embeddings to output a similarity score determining semantic equivalence or entailment (used in bi-encoders like SBERT). Sentence Reordering: Shuffles the order of full sentences in a paragraph; the model must reconstruct the correct logical paragraph flow. Document Rotation: Selects a random token as a rotation point and wraps the beginning of the text to the end; the model must locate the true start and restore the document.
data.sequence--permutation-objectives#Sequenc: Permuted LM (PLM): Samples random factorization orders for predicting tokens while keeping standard positional embeddings, capturing bidirectional context without introducing artificial [MASK] tokens (used by XLNet). Token Classification: Predicts a label (such as Part-of-Speech or Named Entity) for every single token representation simultaneously. Token Deletion: Deletes random tokens entirely without leaving mask tokens; the model must reconstruct the full missing sequence (BART denoising). Token Reordering: Randomly shuffles tokens in the input and trains the model to generate them in the correct original order.

An induction head is a two-layer attention sub-circuit that completes recurring sequences via pattern matching: given context ... [A] [B] ... [A], it predicts that [B] follows the current [A].
Induction heads are considered the primary mechanistic engine driving in-context learning in Transformers. To implement this algorithm across layers, heads must compose by reading each other’s outputs from the residual stream.
data.detecting-composition-in-the-wild#Detect:
To confirm whether two heads H1H_1H1​ and H2H_2H2​ are actually composing rather than operating independently, interpretability researchers use two quantitative tests:
Path Patching (Activation Patching): Run the model on a repeated sequence [A][B] ... [A]. Intercept the output of H1H_1H1​ entering H2H_2H2​’s KKK-input and replace it with corrupted/random activations. If the model’s ability to predict [B] vanishes, H2H_2H2​ causally depends on H1H_1H1​ via K-composition. Matrix Norm Metrics: Measure the Frobenius norm of the product matrix: ∥WK(2)WOV(1)∥F \Vert{} W_K^{(2)} W_{OV}^{(1)} \Vert{}_F ∥WK(2)​WOV(1)​∥F​ Compare this against a baseline where the weight matrices are randomly rotated. In true induction heads, the norm is significantly higher than chance, indicating that WK(2)W_K^{(2)}WK(2)​ specifically aligns with the subspace output by WOV(1)W_{OV}^{(1)}WOV(1)​.

data.step-by-step-how-induction-heads-work#St: The standard induction circuit uses K-Composition (or Q-Composition) to set up the attention pattern, followed by the OV circuit to copy the token.
data.the-algorithmic-goal-of-an-induction-hea:
Suppose the input sequence contains:
…[A]⏟i−1 [B]⏟i … [A]⏟j \dots \underbrace{\text{[A]}}_{i-1} \ \underbrace{\text{[B]}}_{i} \ \dots \ \underbrace{\text{[A]}}_{j} …i−1[A]​​ i[B]​​ … j[A]​​ The current token is at position jjj (which is [A]). To predict that [B] comes next, the network must:
Search backward in the context for an earlier occurrence of token [A]. Find the token that immediately followed that earlier [A] (which is [B] at position iii). Copy [B] to the current prediction at position jjj. A single attention layer cannot do this on its own:
At position iii (where [B] is located), the token [B] has no native awareness that token [A] occurred immediately before it, unless another head or embedding shifted that information into position iii. A 1-layer model can implement a “previous-token head” or a “copy-current-token head”, but it cannot perform “look for previous token matching current token, and extract the next token.” This requires a circuit consisting of at least two heads across two distinct layers:
Head 1 (Layer 0 or early layer): A Previous-Token Head (H1H_1H1​). Head 2 (Layer 1 or downstream layer): An Induction Head (H2H_2H2​).

Mechanistic interpretability treats neural networks not as black boxes, but as computational graphs where weights and activations can be reverse-engineered into human-understandable algorithms.
In the mathematical framework popularized by Anthropic (Elhage et al., A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits), an attention layer is analyzed without the intermediate token dimensions by factoring it into two independent, end-to-end operations:
The QK (Query-Key) circuit: Determines where information moves. The OV (Output-Value) circuit: Determines what information moves.
The attention score between query token at position iii and key token at position jjj (ignoring positional embeddings for a moment) is:

WQK=WQ⊤WK∈Rdmodel×dmodel W_{QK} = W_Q^\top W_K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}} WQK​=WQ⊤​WK​∈Rdmodel​×dmodel​ Rank: WQKW_{QK}WQK​ has a maximum rank of dkd_kdk​ (typically 64 or 128), which is much smaller than dmodeld_{\text{model}}dmodel​ (often 4096+). It acts as a low-rank bilinear form. Interpretation: Given a feature subspace active in the query token (xix_ixi​) and a feature subspace active in the key token (xjx_jxj​), WQKW_{QK}WQK​ directly computes their compatibility score: scorei,j∝xi⊤WQKxj \text{score}_{i,j} \propto x_i^\top W_{QK} x_j scorei,j​∝xi⊤​WQK​xj​ Function: It acts as an addressing system. The QK circuit reads queries and keys from the residual stream and outputs scalar logits over context positions, entirely agnostic to the semantic content being copied or transformed downstream.
Once attention weights Ai,j∈[0,1]A_{i,j} \in [0, 1]Ai,j​∈[0,1] are computed, the head moves information from source position jjj to destination position iii. Looking at a single source position jjj:
contributionj=WO(WVxj)=(WOWV)xj \text{contribution}_j = W_O (W_V x_j) = (W_O W_V) x_j contributionj​=WO​(WV​xj​)=(WO​WV​)xj​ We define the OV matrix as:
WOV=WOWV∈Rdmodel×dmodel W_{OV} = W_O W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}} WOV​=WO​WV​∈Rdmodel​×dmodel​ Rank: Like WQKW_{QK}WQK​, WOVW_{OV}WOV​ has a rank bounded by dv≪dmodeld_v \ll d_{\text{model}}dv​≪dmodel​. Interpretation: WOVW_{OV}WOV​ is a linear map that reads a low-rank subspace from the residual stream at the source position and writes another low-rank subspace directly into the residual stream at the destination position. Function: It dictates what features get extracted from the source and in what direction they are written into the target. Crucially, WOVW_{OV}WOV​ has zero influence on which positions are attended to—it simply specifies the payload.

data.why-factorize-into-qk-and-ov#Why Factori: Separation of Concerns: When analyzing trained models, an attention head can fail or succeed in two distinct ways: Addressing failure: Looking at the wrong token (QK circuit issue). Transmission failure: Looking at the right token but writing the wrong vector or projecting into an orthogonal subspace (OV circuit issue). Eigenvalue/SVD Analysis of WOVW_{OV}WOV​: If WOVW_{OV}WOV​ has positive real eigenvalues, the head acts as an identity/copying head, reinforcing existing token features. If it has negative real eigenvalues, it acts as an inhibition head, erasing or dampening certain directions in the residual stream. Composability Across Layers: In multi-layer models, the output of an early head’s OV circuit feeds into the input of a downstream head’s QK or OV circuit. This leads directly to induction heads and attention composition pathways (QQQ-composition, KKK-composition, and VVV-composition).

data.1-basis--basis-free-operations#1. Basis:
In mechanistic interpretability, operations within a Transformer are categorized by whether their behavior depends on the coordinate system chosen to represent the vector space:
Basis-Free (Rotational Invariance): An operation where rotating the vector space by an orthogonal matrix RRR (R⊤R=IR^\top R = IR⊤R=I) preserves the overall transformation, provided the weights are rotated accordingly. Privileged Basis: An operation where individual coordinate axes (neurons) carry distinct mathematical and semantic meaning that cannot be rotated without breaking the computation.
data.2-superposition#2. Superposition: Superposition is the phenomenon where a neural network represents significantly more independent features than it has dimensions (M≫dM \gg dM≫d).
data.3-double-descent#3. Double Descent:
Double descent is a generalization phenomenon that reconciles classical statistical learning theory with the empirical success of deep, overparameterized neural networks.

data.classical-regime-#Classical Regime ($p \: In classical statistics, as model capacity (number of parameters ppp) increases relative to the number of training samples nnn, bias decreases while variance increases. The test error exhibits the standard U-shaped curve, reaching an optimal trade-off point and then increasing due to overfitting as p→np \to np→n.
data.mlps-introduce-a-privileged-basis#MLPs I:
The MLP blocks break rotational symmetry because activation functions (ReLU\text{ReLU}ReLU, GELU\text{GELU}GELU, SwiGLU\text{SwiGLU}SwiGLU) are applied element-wise:
MLP(x)=Wout σ(Winx+bin) \text{MLP}(x) = W_{\text{out}} \ \sigma(W_{\text{in}} x + b_{\text{in}}) MLP(x)=Wout​ σ(Win​x+bin​) For an arbitrary orthogonal matrix RRR, non-linearities generally do not commute with rotation:
σ(Rz)≠R σ(z) \sigma(R z) \ne R \ \sigma(z) σ(Rz)=R σ(z) Because σ\sigmaσ evaluates each scalar component along the standard coordinate axes independently:
The hidden layer of an MLP has a privileged basis: the coordinate axes correspond directly to individual neurons. In contrast, the residual stream lacks a privileged basis, making it harder to assign individual dimensions to discrete features without techniques like Dictionary Learning / Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs).
data.modern-overparameterized-regime-#Modern:
When capacity extends well beyond the interpolation point (p≫np \gg np≫n), there are infinitely many parameter configurations that achieve zero training error. Optimizers like Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) implicitly regularize the solution by selecting the interpolating function with the minimum norm (e.g., minimum L2L_2L2​ norm in weights): w∗=arg⁡min⁡w∥w∥s.t.Xw=y w^* = \arg\min_w \Vert{}w\Vert{} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad Xw = y w∗=argwmin​∥w∥s.t.Xw=y As parameter count increases further, the space of zero-loss interpolators expands, allowing SGD to find smoother, lower-norm functions that interpolate the training points while generalizing effectively. Double descent manifests across three primary dimensions:
Model-wise Double Descent: Varying the width or depth of the architecture. Epoch-wise Double Descent: Prolonged training where error drops, rises, and drops again. Sample-wise Double Descent: Varying dataset size nnn for a fixed model size ppp.
data.polysemanticity#Polysemanticity: Superposition directly causes polysemanticity: because feature directions are not aligned with standard basis vectors, individual neurons (the basis vectors) end up projecting onto multiple unrelated feature directions. Inspecting a single neuron activation reveals that it activates for multiple distinct, unrelated concepts.

Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), introduced by DeepSeek, solves a core bottleneck in Transformer inference: the massive size and memory bandwidth cost of the KV Cache.
Chris McCormick
While Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) reduces KV heads at the cost of model expressiveness, MLA achieves extreme compression without losing representational capacity by using low-rank latent projections and algebraic weight absorption.
Chris McCormick
data.1-why-standard-multi-head-attention-mha-:
For an input token vector xt∈Rd\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^dxt​∈Rd across nhn_hnh​ heads, each head generates query, key, and value vectors of dimension dhd_hdh​:
qt,i=xtWiQ,kt,i=xtWiK,vt,i=xtWiV(i=1,…,nh) \mathbf{q}_{t,i} = \mathbf{x}_t \mathbf{W}_i^Q, \quad \mathbf{k}_{t,i} = \mathbf{x}_t \mathbf{W}_i^K, \quad \mathbf{v}_{t,i} = \mathbf{x}_t \mathbf{W}_i^V \quad (i = 1, \dots, n_h) qt,i​=xt​WiQ​,kt,i​=xt​WiK​,vt,i​=xt​WiV​(i=1,…,nh​) During autoregressive generation, we must store all past keys and values in memory:
KV Cache per token=2×nh×dh numbers \text{KV Cache per token} = 2 \times n_h \times d_h \text{ numbers} KV Cache per token=2×nh​×dh​ numbers For large models (e.g., 128 heads, head dimension 128), that is over 32,000 floats per token, dominating memory footprint and memory-bus bandwidth.

The transition from the dense DeepSeek-LLM 67B to DeepSeekMoE marks the architectural pivot that defined all of DeepSeek’s later flagship models (DeepSeek-V2, V3, and R1).
While standard Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures—like Mixtral 8x7B or Switch Transformer—simply swap dense Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) for a small bank of large sub-networks, DeepSeek discovered severe structural flaws in this setup. DeepSeekMoE re-architected the MoE layer around two core principles: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared expert isolation.
data.1-the-bottlenecks-of-traditional-moe-arc:
Conventional MoEs divide the FFN layer into NNN experts (typically N=8N = 8N=8) and activate the top-KKK experts (typically K=2K = 2K=2) per token. DeepSeek identified two fundamental limitations in this paradigm:
Knowledge Hybridity (Lack of Specialization): Because K=2K=2K=2 is so small, each routed expert is forced to learn a vast, overlapping mixture of broad concepts (e.g., syntax, grammar, basic facts) rather than truly specializing in narrow domains (e.g., Python recursion, organic chemistry, or legal reasoning). Combinatorial Constraint: With N=8N=8N=8 and K=2K=2K=2, the router can only produce: (82)=28 possible expert combinations \binom{8}{2} = 28 \text{ possible expert combinations} (28​)=28 possible expert combinations This severely caps the expressive capacity of the model for diverse tokens. Knowledge Redundancy: Multiple experts end up wasting capacity re-learning the exact same ubiquitous, cross-domain background knowledge.
data.2-the-core-mechanics-of-fine-grained-rou:
DeepSeek addressed this by dividing the standard expert size into significantly smaller slices and activating proportionally more of them, keeping total activated FLOPs constant.
Traditional MoE (e.g., Mixtral 8x7B): Input Token ──► [ Router: Top-2 of 8 ] ──► [ Large Expert 1 ] + [ Large Expert 4 ] Combinations: 28 DeepSeekMoE Fine-Grained: Input Token ──► [ Shared Experts (Always ON) ] ───────────────┐ └──► [ Router: Top-m of N (e.g., Top-8 of 64) ] ──┴──► Combined Output Combinations: > 4.4 Billion
data.3-transitioning-the-architecture-dense-6:
To prove the paradigm, DeepSeek designed comparative models directly against the DeepSeek-LLM dense baselines:
Architecture Metric DeepSeek-LLM (Dense Baseline) DeepSeekMoE 16B Scaled DeepSeekMoE (V2 Base) Total Parameters 7B (or 67B) 16.4B 236B Activated Parameters / Token 7B (or 67B) 2.8B 21B Routing Setup None (Dense FFN) 1 Shared + 64 Routed (Top-8 active) 2 Shared + 160 Routed (Top-6 active) Compute Efficiency Baseline (1×1\times1×) ~40% compute of 7B dense ~30% compute of 67B dense Performance Benchmark Baseline Matches/beats 7B dense Surpasses 67B dense
data.a-fine-grained-expert-segmentation#A. Fi:
Instead of assigning an intermediate hidden dimension dffnd_{\text{ffn}}dffn​ to a single expert, DeepSeek divides it by a splitting factor mmm:
Each expert’s intermediate dimension becomes dffnm\frac{d_{\text{ffn}}}{m}mdffn​​. To preserve the exact same compute budget per token, the number of activated routed experts scales from KKK to m×Km \times Km×K. Total available experts increases from NNN to m×Nm \times Nm×N. The Combinatorial Explosion:
If m=4m = 4m=4, an N=16,K=2N=16, K=2N=16,K=2 system becomes N=64,K=8N=64, K=8N=64,K=8:
(648)≈4.42×109 combinations \binom{64}{8} \approx 4.42 \times 10^9 \text{ combinations} (864​)≈4.42×109 combinations By expanding the pool of available pathways from 28 to over 4.4 billion, the model can assemble specialized micro-circuits custom-tailored to nuanced token contexts, drastically reducing knowledge hybridity.
data.b-shared-expert-isolation#B. Shared Expe:
To eliminate redundancy, DeepSeek isolates a fixed set of KsK_sKs​ shared experts that remain permanently active for every single token, bypassing the router entirely:
ht=ut+∑i=1KsFFNishared(ut)+∑j∈Top-Krgj,t⋅FFNjrouted(ut) \mathbf{h}_t = \mathbf{u}_t + \sum_{i=1}^{K_s} \text{FFN}_i^{\text{shared}}(\mathbf{u}_t) + \sum_{j \in \text{Top-}K_r} g_{j,t} \cdot \text{FFN}_j^{\text{routed}}(\mathbf{u}_t) ht​=ut​+i=1∑Ks​​FFNishared​(ut​)+j∈Top-Kr​∑​gj,t​⋅FFNjrouted​(ut​) Where:
ut\mathbf{u}_tut​ is the input representation of token ttt. FFNishared\text{FFN}_i^{\text{shared}}FFNishared​ processes universal common-sense patterns, punctuation, grammar, and generic sentence framing. FFNjrouted\text{FFN}_j^{\text{routed}}FFNjrouted​ contains the fine-grained routed experts, which now only activate for domain-specific features. gj,tg_{j,t}gj,t​ is the normalized routing weight computed over the selected top-KrK_rKr​ candidates.
data.why-the-transition-succeeded#Why the Tra: Parameter Decoupling: In the dense 67B model, scaling knowledge required scaling FLOPs linearly on every token. With fine-grained MoE, DeepSeek decoupled memory capacity (total parameters) from inference execution cost (active parameters). No Routing Collapse: Smaller, fine-grained experts combined with dedicated shared experts eliminated routing bottlenecks where one or two “celebrity experts” hog all the tokens, leading to far more uniform token distribution across hardware devices. This fine-grained routing blueprint, validated in the January 2024 paper, served directly as the execution engine for DeepSeek-V2 and V3, allowing V3 to scale to 671B total parameters while activating only 37B per token.

data: DeepSeek-LLM: Scaling Open-Source Language Models with Longtermism (January 5, 2024) serves as DeepSeek’s foundational technical paper. It established both the empirical methodology and the engineering infrastructure that later underpinned models like DeepSeekMoE, DeepSeek-V2/V3, and DeepSeek-R1.
data.1-motivation-why-longtermism#1. Motivati:
At the time of release, many open-source models scaled parameters by strictly copying LLaMA or following standard Chinchilla-scaling recipes without testing the limits of data-to-parameter saturation. DeepSeek approached scaling with two specific long-term goals:
Rethink Scaling Laws Under Variable Data Quality: Systematically derive how hyperparameter selection (batch size, learning rate) and compute-optimal parameter-to-data allocation shift as data quality improves. Build Continuous Pre-Training Infrastructure: Move away from one-off, static model checkpoints by introducing training dynamics (such as multi-step learning rate schedules) that allow weights to be reused and expanded as more high-quality data arrives.
DeepSeek adopted a modern dense Transformer backbone with targeted structural modifications:
Specification DeepSeek 7B DeepSeek 67B Layers 30 95 Hidden Dimension (dmodeld_{\text{model}}dmodel​) 4096 8192 Attention Heads (Q/KVQ/KVQ/KV) 32 / 32 (MHA) 64 / 8 (GQA) Intermediate FFN Dim 11,008 27,648 Context Length 4,096 tokens 4,096 tokens Vocabulary Size 102,400 tokens 102,400 tokens
data.4-training-dynamics--the-multi-step-lear:
Most pre-trained LLMs utilize a Cosine Learning Rate schedule with warmup, which decays the learning rate to near-zero at a pre-set step count. The paper points out two drawbacks of cosine decay:
It commits the team to an exact token budget upfront. Extending training past the schedule’s end requires clumsy restarts or causes loss instability. To support their “longtermism” philosophy, DeepSeek introduced a Multi-Step Learning Rate Scheduler for pre-training:
Warmup: Linear warmup over the first 2,000 steps to peak LR. Constant High LR: Maintained steady peak learning rate through 80% of the training budget. Step 1 Decay: At 80% of tokens, LR steps down to 31.6% (1/101/\sqrt{10}1/10​) of maximum. Step 2 Decay: At 90% of tokens, LR steps down to 10% of maximum. The authors proved that this multi-step schedule achieves a final validation loss virtually identical to a cosine schedule, while keeping the model in a high-learning state for the majority of the training run so additional token sets can be appended without destabilizing convergence.
data.5-pre-training-corpus--alignment-sft--dp: 2.0 Trillion Tokens: Pre-trained on a bilingual dataset (English and Chinese). The data pipeline was organized into three distinct phases: deduplication, filtering (linguistic heuristics and information-density scoring), and remixing (balancing code, scientific text, and informal forum discussions). Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): Fine-tuned across ~1.5 million instruction instances covering coding, conversational dialogue, reasoning, and multi-turn math. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO): DeepSeek applied DPO directly to the SFT base using a batch size of 512 and a learning rate of 5×10−65 \times 10^{-6}5×10−6. They found that DPO notably boosted open-ended generation, nuance, and human evaluation scores while preserving performance on standard deterministic benchmarks.
data.6-results-and-benchmark-impact#6. Result: Beating LLaMA-2 70B: Despite having slightly fewer parameters (67B vs. 70B) and being trained on 2T tokens, DeepSeek-LLM 67B outperformed LLaMA-2 70B across coding (HumanEval), mathematics (GSM8K, MATH), and standard reasoning benchmarks. Chat Competitiveness: In Chinese and English open-ended evaluations, DeepSeek-LLM 67B Chat surpassed GPT-3.5, marking DeepSeek’s entrance as a top-tier open-weight model developer.
data.a-hyperparameter-scaling-laws#A. Hyperpa:
Before scaling up to 7B and 67B parameter models, the authors evaluated hundreds of small-scale training runs across compute budgets from 101710^{17}1017 to 102010^{20}1020 FLOPs to establish exact power-law trends for learning rate (η\etaη) and batch size (BBB):
Optimal Batch Size (BBB): Monotonically grows as compute budget (CCC) increases. Optimal Learning Rate (η\etaη): Monotonically decays as compute budget (CCC) increases. Tolerance Basin: Generalization loss remained within 0.25% of the theoretical optimum across a relatively broad hyperparameter envelope, giving engineering flexibility when fitting models onto cluster hardware.
data.b-the-impact-of-data-quality-on-scaling-:
A major discovery in this paper was that data quality fundamentally changes the optimal ratio between parameters (NNN) and data tokens (DDD):
When data quality is relatively low or noisy, optimal compute allocation favors scaling model size faster than token count, as larger models better absorb noisy signals. As data quality improves via aggressive filtering, deduplication, and synthetic curation, the optimal frontier shifts: the model can extract information efficiently from significantly more tokens per parameter without premature loss saturation. This justified training their 7B and 67B models on 2 trillion tokens—well beyond the canonical 20 tokens-per-parameter Chinchilla ratio.
data.structural-highlights#Structural Highlig: 95-Layer Depth for 67B: Rather than using the typical 80-layer layout seen in models like LLaMA-2 70B, DeepSeek opted for 95 layers. This odd layer depth was specifically selected to divide evenly across 3D-parallel pipeline stages while favoring depth-over-width inductive bias for symbolic and logical reasoning. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA): 67B used 8 KV heads with 64 query heads (8:1 ratio) to cut KV cache memory consumption during decoding, whereas the 7B model retained standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA). Pre-Norm + SwiGLU + RoPE: Followed standard pre-normalization with RMSNorm, SwiGLU non-linearities, and Rotary Position Embeddings.

The paper “DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model” (DeepSeek-AI, May 2024) introduced a 236B-parameter Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) transformer that drastically lowered training costs and inference serving overhead. With 236B total parameters and only 21B activated parameters per token, DeepSeek-V2 achieved performance competitive with contemporary closed and open front-runners while cutting KV cache memory requirements by 93.3% and boosting generation throughput by 5.76×.
Its core architectural breakthroughs are Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) and the DeepSeekMoE architecture.
data.1-multi-head-latent-attention-mla#1. Mul:
Standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) run into heavy memory bandwidth bottlenecks during autoregressive generation because they must cache uncompressed Key and Value states across all layers. GQA reduces cache size by forcing heads to share keys and values, which can compromise representational capacity.

data.2-deepseekmoe-architecture#2. DeepSeekMo:
Conventional MoEs (such as Mixtral 8x7B) split the MLP into a few large experts (e.g., 8 experts, choosing top-2). DeepSeek argued that this granularity is too coarse, limiting the combinatorial combinations of knowledge and causing individual experts to overlap in responsibility.
DeepSeek-V2 implements two foundational MoE principles:
┌───────── Input Token x ─────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Shared Experts │ │ Routed Experts │ │ (Always Activated) │ │ (Fine-Grained Top-m) │ │ [Expert 1, 2, ...] │ │ [Expert 1, 2, ..., N] │ └───────────┬───────────┘ └───────────┬───────────┘ │ │ └───────────────┬─────────────────┘ ▼ Fused Output Fine-Grained Expert Segmentation: Instead of NNN standard-sized experts, DeepSeek divides expert capacity into mNmNmN smaller experts (each having 1/m1/m1/m the hidden dimension) and activates mkmkmk of them. DeepSeek-V2 scales this to 160 routed experts, selecting 6 routed experts per token. This vastly expands the combinatorial flexibility of expert coordination without increasing active compute. Dedicated Shared Experts: A subset of experts (2 shared experts) is permanently active for every token, bypassing the router. Why this matters: In standard MoEs, generalist knowledge (syntax, standard grammar, formatting) ends up redundantly learned across many routed experts. Isolating shared parameters forces common representations into the shared experts, freeing routed experts to specialize strictly in distinct semantic domains. The output for token xxx is:

data.4-load-balancing--training-dynamics#4. L:
To prevent routing collapse across 160 fine-grained experts, DeepSeek-V2 avoided device-level hard capacity factors (which drop tokens and hurt quality) and instead used a multi-tier loss formulation:
Expert-Level Balance Loss (Lexp\mathcal{L}_{\text{exp}}Lexp​): Penalizes routing probability skew across individual experts. Device-Level Balance Loss (Ldev\mathcal{L}_{\text{dev}}Ldev​): Groups experts across physical GPUs/nodes and penalizes imbalanced aggregate computation across accelerator devices, minimizing inter-device pipeline stalls. Communication Optimization: By co-locating groups of routed experts and overlapping all-to-all communication with token computation kernels, the communication overhead typical of fine-grained MoE dispatch was mitigated on dual-ring cluster topologies.
Inference Economy: Standard MoEs reduce training compute relative to parameter size, but during decoding they still suffer under full KV cache memory limits. MLA directly decoupled sequence memory from head width, enabling massive batch sizes and 128K context scaling on modest hardware clusters. Foundation for V3 and R1: The twin innovations of MLA and fine-grained shared/routed MoE established the blueprint carried forward into DeepSeek-Coder-V2, DeepSeek-V3, and the DeepSeek-R1 reasoning series.

Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) is an architectural framework introduced by DeepSeek-AI (mHC: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections, arXiv:2512.24880) designed to scale and stabilize the macro-architecture of deep networks—particularly large language models.
It addresses fundamental training instabilities in multi-stream residual networks by enforcing geometric constraints on how residual information is routed across layers.
data.1-background-from-resnets-to-hyper-conne:
In standard Transformers and ResNets, a layer update follows a single residual stream:
xl+1=xl+F(xl,Wl) \mathbf{x}_{l+1} = \mathbf{x}_l + \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}_l, \mathcal{W}_l) xl+1​=xl​+F(xl​,Wl​) This identity shortcut (xl\mathbf{x}_lxl​) guarantees that:
Forward signals can pass unaltered without vanishing or exploding. Gradients can flow backward across deep layers without attenuation (∂xl+1∂xl≈I\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{l+1}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_l} \approx \mathbf{I}∂xl​∂xl+1​​≈I).
data.2-the-problem-with-unconstrained-hyper-c:
While HC demonstrated empirical benefits on shallow setups, it breaks the identity mapping assumption in deep architectures:
In standard HC, the inter-stream matrix Hlres\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}}Hlres​ is an unconstrained linear transformation. As signals propagate through LLL layers, the effective residual path is governed by the cumulative matrix product: ∏l=1LHlres \prod_{l=1}^L \mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}} l=1∏L​Hlres​ Without constraints, eigenvalues deviating slightly from 1.01.01.0 compound exponentially. This causes: Forward signal explosion or collapse: Feature norms either blow up or fade to zero. Gradient instability: Backward gradients along the residual paths explode or vanish, preventing convergence in very deep or large-scale models.
data.3-deepseeks-solution-manifold-constraint:
DeepSeek’s core insight is that network stability is a geometric property. Instead of allowing arbitrary linear mixing, mHC constrains the connection matrices onto specific mathematical manifolds:
``` ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ Input Streams (x_l) │ └──────┬─────────────────┬──────┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ H_res (Doubly Stochastic) H_pre (Convex Weights) via Sinkhorn-Knopp │ │ ▼ │ ┌──────────────┐ │ │ Sub-Layer F │ │ └──────┬───────┘ │ │ │ ▼ │ H_post │ │ ▼ ▼ ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ Output Streams (x_{l+1}) │ └───────────────────────────────┘
#### A. Doubly Stochastic Residual Mapping ($\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}}$) mHC constrains $\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}}$ to the **Birkhoff polytope** (the set of doubly stochastic matrices): 1. **Non-negativity**: $\mathbf{H}_{ij} \ge 0$ (prevents destructive interference or sign inversion). 2. **Row Sums $= 1$**: $\sum_j \mathbf{H}_{ij} = 1$ ensures that the forward operation $\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}} \mathbf{x}_l$ is a strict convex combination of residual streams, conserving forward signal scale. 3. **Column Sums $= 1$**: $\sum_i \mathbf{H}_{ij} = 1$ ensures that during backpropagation, the incoming adjoint gradients are also convexly distributed, preventing gradient explosion. **Key Mathematical Invariant (Closure):** Because the product of any two doubly stochastic matrices is itself doubly stochastic, the compound residual path across arbitrary layers: $$ \mathbf{M}_{1 \to L} = \prod_{l=1}^L \mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}} $$ remains strictly doubly stochastic. This guarantees that identity-like conservation holds across arbitrary depth without norm distortion. #### B. Projection via Sinkhorn–Knopp To map unconstrained learned logits $\mathbf{S}_l \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ onto the Birkhoff polytope in a differentiable manner, DeepSeek applies the **Sinkhorn–Knopp algorithm**: 1. Compute elementwise exponentiation $\mathbf{P}^{(0)} = \exp(\mathbf{S}_l)$. 2. Alternately normalize rows and columns for a small number of iterations (e.g., 3–5 steps): $$ \mathbf{P}^{(k+1/2)} = \mathbf{D}_{\text{row}}^{-1} \mathbf{P}^{(k)}, \quad \mathbf{P}^{(k+1)} = \mathbf{P}^{(k+1/2)} \mathbf{D}_{\text{col}}^{-1} $$ *(Note: The paper also explores orthostochastic matrices derived via iterative Newton–Schulz steps as an alternative unitary-preserving geometry).* #### C. Non-Negative Pre- and Post-Projections $\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{pre}}$ and $\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{post}}$ are mapped via functions like softmax or non-negative normalizations to ensure that reading from and writing to the residual streams acts as smooth interpolation rather than divergent linear projection. ### 4\. Systems Optimization & Empirical Findings Expanding residual channels multiplies the volume of activations transferred between layers, which could otherwise introduce substantial memory bandwidth and runtime bottlenecks. DeepSeek addresses this through co-designed systems engineering: - **Kernel Fusion & Custom DSLs:** Using TileLang, mHC fuses the Sinkhorn–Knopp iterations, tensor contractions, and layer-norm operations into unified GPU kernels. - **Overhead at Scale:** For an expansion factor of $n = 4$ streams, mHC adds only ~6.7% wall-clock training overhead while providing strictly stable convergence. - **Scaling Behavior:** Models trained with mHC exhibit improved loss convergence rates compared to standard single-stream baselines at equal compute budgets, demonstrating that multi-stream residual routing can be scaled without architectural degradation.
data.the-hyper-connections-hc-generalization#:
To increase capacity without altering internal block FLOPs, recent work introduced Hyper-Connections (HC). Instead of a single residual vector, HC expands the residual pathway into nnn parallel streams:
xl+1=Hlresxl+(Hlpost)⊤F(Hlprexl,Wl) \mathbf{x}_{l+1} = \mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}} \mathbf{x}_l + (\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{post}})^\top \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{pre}} \mathbf{x}_l, \mathcal{W}_l) xl+1​=Hlres​xl​+(Hlpost​)⊤F(Hlpre​xl​,Wl​) Where:
Hlpre∈R1×n\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{pre}} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times n}Hlpre​∈R1×n: Reads and linearly mixes features from the nnn streams to feed into the computational block F\mathcal{F}F (e.g., Attention or FFN). Hlpost∈R1×n\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{post}} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times n}Hlpost​∈R1×n: Writes the output of the block back across the nnn streams. Hlres∈Rn×n\mathbf{H}_l^{\text{res}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}Hlres​∈Rn×n: Inter-stream residual routing matrix that mixes parallel streams directly.

The paper “Mixtral of Experts” (Jiang et al., Mistral AI, Jan 2024) introduced Mixtral 8x7B, a Sparse Mixture of Experts (SMoE) decoder-only transformer that redefined efficiency tradeoffs in open-weight models.
arXiv
data.1-high-level-architecture--parameter-mec:
Despite the “8x7B” naming, Mixtral is not an ensemble of eight distinct 7B models.
Shared Parameters: The self-attention blocks, layer normalizations, and input/output embeddings are fully shared across the entire model. Sparse Components: Only the standard Feed-Forward Network (FFN / MLP) blocks inside each transformer layer are replaced with 8 parallel expert networks. Open Laboratory Parameter Breakdown: Total Parameters: ~46.7B. Open Laboratory Active Parameters per Token: ~12.9B. Open Laboratory During inference, it computes at the latency and FLOP cost of a ~13B dense model while matching or outperforming Llama 2 70B and GPT-3.5 across reasoning, code, and math. Mistral
For each token embedding x∈Rdx \in \mathbb{R}^dx∈Rd entering the MoE block at layer lll:
Routing / Gating: A trainable linear gate Wg∈RE×dW_g \in \mathbb{R}^{E \times d}Wg​∈RE×d (where number of experts E=8E = 8E=8) computes routing logits: H(x)=x⋅WgT H(x) = x \cdot W_g^T H(x)=x⋅WgT​ Top-2 Selection & Normalization: Mixtral selects the top k=2k = 2k=2 highest-scoring experts. The gating distribution over the chosen subset Top-2(H(x))\text{Top-2}(H(x))Top-2(H(x)) is computed via a Softmax over only those top-2 logits: Open Laboratory Pi(x)={exp⁡(H(x)i)∑j∈Top-2(H(x))exp⁡(H(x)j)if i∈Top-2(H(x))0otherwise P_i(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{\exp(H(x)_i)}{\sum_{j \in \text{Top-2}(H(x))} \exp(H(x)_j)} & \text{if } i \in \text{Top-2}(H(x)) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Pi​(x)={∑j∈Top-2(H(x))​exp(H(x)j​)exp(H(x)i​)​0​if i∈Top-2(H(x))otherwise​ Additive Aggregation: The output of the MoE block is the weighted sum of outputs from the two selected experts: y=∑i=1EPi(x)⋅Experti(x) y = \sum_{i=1}^{E} P_i(x) \cdot \text{Expert}_i(x) y=i=1∑E​Pi​(x)⋅Experti​(x) Each expert is an independent SwiGLU MLP: Experti(x)=(Swish(xW1,i)⊙xW3,i)W2,i \text{Expert}_i(x) = \left(\text{Swish}(x W_{1,i}) \odot x W_{3,i}\right) W_{2,i} Experti​(x)=(Swish(xW1,i​)⊙xW3,i​)W2,i​
data.3-load-balancing--training-dynamics#3. L:
MoE routing networks naturally suffer from a “winner-takes-all” failure mode, where a handful of experts receive all traffic while others starve, wasting parameter capacity.
Auxiliary Loss: To prevent expert collapse and ensure load balancing across GPUs/experts, Mixtral employs an auxiliary routing loss: Laux=α⋅E∑i=1Efi⋅Pi \mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha \cdot E \sum_{i=1}^E f_i \cdot P_i Laux​=α⋅Ei=1∑E​fi​⋅Pi​ where fif_ifi​ is the fraction of tokens in the batch dispatched to expert iii, and PiP_iPi​ is the average routing probability assigned to expert iii. Co-training: Unlike methods that upcycle pre-trained dense checkpoints into MoEs, Mixtral trained the router and expert weights jointly from scratch.
data.4-empirical-routing-analysis-how-do-expe:
One of the most notable analyses in the paper is examining what the experts actually specialize in:
Syntactic vs. Semantic Specialization: In the early and late layers, token routing correlates heavily with syntactic/grammatical structure (e.g., specific punctuation, indentation, whitespace, common function words). Open Laboratory In the middle layers, routing displays higher semantic divergence, but not a clean topic-by-topic division (i.e., there is no single “Python expert” or “history expert”). Open Laboratory Temporal Locality: Tokens appearing close to each other in the sequence frequently route to the same expert due to contextual similarity in hidden states. Multilingual Uniformity: Experts do not cleanly segregate by language; representations are shared across languages for abstract reasoning.
data.5-systems--inference-implementation#5. S:
The primary challenge of sparse MoEs is hardware utilization:
Memory Footprint: Running Mixtral requires keeping all ~47B weights in VRAM (requiring ~90–100 GB in FP16/BF16, or ~24–30 GB with 4-bit / AWQ / GPTQ quantization). Open Laboratory Dynamic Batching & Kernel Efficiency: In standard dense layers, matrix multiplications are contiguous. In MoEs, dynamic token-to-expert assignments lead to irregular memory layouts. MegaBlocks Integration: Mixtral’s open deployment relied on integrating MegaBlocks block-sparse matrix multiplication kernels into serving frameworks (vLLM). This avoids padding overheads and efficiently executes dynamic top-2 routing without dropping tokens. arXiv
data.6-key-takeaways#6. Key Takeaways: Compute vs. Memory Disconnect: Mixtral proved that model scale can be decoupled from per-token compute: you pay the memory capacity price of a ~47B model to get the throughput and compute latency of a ~13B model. Open Laboratory Open-Weight Milestone: It demonstrated that properly regularized, from-scratch SMoE scaling could match dense flagship baselines (Llama 2 70B) at a fraction of active inference FLOPs.

Self-attention in Transformers is permutation-equivariant: without position information, the model treats a sequence as an unordered bag of tokens. Positional encodings break this symmetry, giving tokens an address or a distance metric.
Abhik Sarkar
Positional embeddings in LLMs fall into three broad architectural families: Absolute, Relative, and Rotary / Bias-based hybrids.
These assign a fixed or learned coordinate vector to each exact index (0,1,2,…,N0, 1, 2, \dots, N0,1,2,…,N) and add it directly to the token embedding before feeding it into the first transformer layer: xi=ei+pix_i = e_i + p_ixi​=ei​+pi​.
Sinusoidal Positional Encoding (Fixed APE): Mechanism: Introduced in the original Transformer (Attention Is All You Need). Uses interleaved geometric sine and cosine waves across embedding dimensions: PE(pos,2i)=sin⁡(pos100002i/d),PE(pos,2i+1)=cos⁡(pos100002i/d) PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right), \quad PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right) PE(pos,2i)​=sin(100002i/dpos​),PE(pos,2i+1)​=cos(100002i/dpos​) Strengths: Zero learned parameters; theoretically represents relative shifts via trigonometric identities. Limitations: Added directly at the input, tangling positional information with semantic embeddings. Does not extrapolate reliably beyond the training sequence length. Wayland Zhang+ 1 Learned Absolute Embeddings: Mechanism: Used in models like BERT, GPT-2, and OPT. Treats positions as a lookup table of trainable parameters matrix Wpos∈RLmax⁡×dW_{pos} \in \mathbb{R}^{L_{\max} \times d}Wpos​∈RLmax​×d. Strengths: Adapts directly to the pretraining corpus data distribution. Limitations: Hard ceiling on sequence length (Lmax⁡L_{\max}Lmax​). It cannot process token Lmax⁡+1L_{\max} + 1Lmax​+1 without structural alterations or interpolation.
data.2-relative-positional-encodings-rpe#2. R:
Rather than caring where a token sits in the whole document, RPE cares about pairwise distance (i−j)(i - j)(i−j) between the query token iii and key token jjj.
liveBook · Manning - Manning Publications
Shaw’s Relative Positional Encoding: Mechanism: Modifies the attention score and value aggregation by adding learned bias vectors corresponding to the clipped relative distance clip(i−j,−k,k)\text{clip}(i - j, -k, k)clip(i−j,−k,k). Strengths: Translates easily across sequence lengths; reflects the intuition that local syntactic context matters more than global indices. Limitations: Adds memory and compute overhead when forming per-head attention matrices; tricky to cache efficiently for fast autoregressive generation. T5 Relative Bias: Mechanism: Simplifies Shaw’s approach by directly adding a scalar bias bi−jb_{i-j}bi−j​ to the attention logit: Attentionij=qikj⊤d+bi−j \text{Attention}_{ij} = \frac{q_i k_j^\top}{\sqrt{d}} + b_{i-j} Attentionij​=d​qi​kj⊤​​+bi−j​ Positions are bucketed logarithmically so that nearby tokens have fine-grained distance bins, while far tokens share coarse bins. Strengths: Extremely lightweight scalar addition; scales to long contexts with few parameters. Transformer-XL / DeBERTa Relative Disentangled Encoding: Mechanism: Decomposes attention into four disentangled terms: content-to-content, content-to-position, position-to-content, and position-to-position. Strengths: Stronger representations for masked language modeling and natural language understanding.
data.3-modern-multiplicative--attention-bias-:
Modern autoregressive LLMs avoid adding vectors at the bottom layer, injecting position information directly into attention heads.
RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding): Mechanism: Used by LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, and DeepSeek. Instead of adding vectors, it rotates 2D slices of query and key vectors by an angle proportional to the position index mmm: qm=RΘ,mWqxm,kn=RΘ,nWkxn \mathbf{q}_m = \mathbf{R}_{\Theta, m} \mathbf{W}_q \mathbf{x}_m, \quad \mathbf{k}_n = \mathbf{R}_{\Theta, n} \mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{x}_n qm​=RΘ,m​Wq​xm​,kn​=RΘ,n​Wk​xn​ When computing qm⊤kn\mathbf{q}_m^\top \mathbf{k}_nqm⊤​kn​, the inner product naturally simplifies to an expression that depends purely on (m−n)(m - n)(m−n). Strengths: Preserves vector norms, integrates with KV-caching with zero overhead, and allows context expansion via frequency scaling (e.g., RoPE-NTK, YaRN). ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases): Mechanism: Used in BLOOM and MPT. Completely removes position embeddings. Instead, it adds a static, non-learned penalty proportional to distance directly to the attention logits: Attentioni,j=qikj⊤d−m⋅∣i−j∣ \text{Attention}_{i, j} = \frac{q_i k_j^\top}{\sqrt{d}} - m \cdot \vert{}i - j\vert{} Attentioni,j​=d​qi​kj⊤​​−m⋅∣i−j∣ where m=2−8h/Hm = 2^{-8h/H}m=2−8h/H is a fixed geometric slope unique to each attention head hhh. Strengths: Zero learned position weights; achieves smooth zero-shot length extrapolation out of the box. Limitations: Imposes a strict monotonic decay (local attention bias), which can hinder tasks needing long-range global reasoning. MetricGate NoPE (No Positional Encoding): Mechanism: Eliminates positional encodings entirely. How it works: In causal decoder-only models, the autoregressive lower-triangular causal mask and causal scratchpad provide an implicit directional order. Usage: Primarily used in research settings; performs surprisingly well on specific algorithmic and recurrent tasks, though it generally lags behind RoPE on standard natural language benchmarks.

KV-Cache Friendly: Tokens can be encoded on-the-fly and cached at inference without needing to recalculate past tokens when the context grows. data.the-intuition#The Intuition:
In standard attention, positional information is either:
Added to inputs (x+pmx + p_mx+pm​), which entangles semantics with coordinates and dilutes deeper in the network. Injected as relative distance biases into attention logits, which can add computational overhead and break clean KV-cache management. RoPE takes a geometric approach:
Imagine a 2D plane. If you have two vectors q\mathbf{q}q and k\mathbf{k}k, rotating q\mathbf{q}q by an angle α\alphaα and k\mathbf{k}k by β\betaβ changes their dot product based strictly on the difference β−α\beta - \alphaβ−α. The length (norm) of the vectors is preserved because rotations are orthogonal transformations. The two foundational papers that established and refined LLM scaling laws are:
Kaplan et al. (OpenAI, 2020): “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models” GitHub Hoffmann et al. (DeepMind, 2022): “Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models” (commonly known as the Chinchilla paper) Analytics Vidhya Below is a detailed synthesis of all the major insights from both papers.
data.1-kaplan-et-al-openai-2020-insights#1. K: Kaplan et al. provided the first empirical foundation showing that language model performance improves predictably according to strict power laws across many orders of magnitude.
data.2-hoffmann-et-al--chinchilla-deepmind-20:
DeepMind re-examined Kaplan et al.’s findings by training over 400 models (ranging from 70M to 16B parameters on up to 500B tokens). They discovered that OpenAI’s original learning rate schedules and hyperparameter setups artificially penalized smaller models trained on large token counts, leading to flawed conclusions.
GitHub
data.direct-comparison--modern-impact#Direct: Metric / Dimension Kaplan et al. (OpenAI 2020) Hoffmann et al. / Chinchilla (DeepMind 2022) Compute Scaling Strategy Favor Model Size (N∝C0.73N\propto C^{0.73}N∝C0.73) over Data (D∝C0.27D\propto C^{0.27}D∝C0.27) Equal Proportional Scaling (N∝C0.5N\propto C^{0.5}N∝C0.5, D∝C0.5D\propto C^{0.5}D∝C0.5) Token-to-Parameter Ratio ~1.7 to 5 tokens per parameter ~20 tokens per parameter Model Paradigm Example GPT-3 (175B params, 300B tokens) Chinchilla (70B params, 1.4T tokens) Primary Takeaway Train larger models and stop early. Train smaller models on much more data.
data.key-insights#Key Insights:: Performance is highly predictable: Test loss (LLL) scales smoothly as a power law with compute budget (CCC), model size (NNN), and dataset size (DDD): GitHub L(N)∝N−αN,L(D)∝D−αD,L(C)∝C−αC L(N) \propto N^{-\alpha_N}, \quad L(D) \propto D^{-\alpha_D}, \quad L(C) \propto C^{-\alpha_C} L(N)∝N−αN​,L(D)∝D−αD​,L(C)∝C−αC​ Architecture shape barely matters: Specific design details—such as depth vs. width, feed-forward dimensions, or number of attention heads—have minimal effect on final performance compared to overall parameter count. GitHub Bigger models are more sample-efficient: Larger models learn faster and achieve a target loss using fewer total tokens than smaller models. GitHub “Bigger is Better” allocation (The Flaw): Kaplan et al. concluded that when compute increases, most of the new budget should go toward increasing model size (NNN), while data size (DDD) needs to grow only slowly. arXiv Their rule: Increase model size by ∼73%\sim 73\%∼73% and dataset size by only ∼27%\sim 27\%∼27% for each doubling of compute. Early stopping & undertraining: They suggested it is optimal to train massive models for relatively few steps and stop training long before full convergence. GitHub Downstream capability gap: Smooth, continuous scaling predicts cross-entropy loss improvement, but does not explicitly predict qualitative “emergent” capabilities (like few-shot reasoning).
data.key-insights-1#Key Insights:: The 1:1 Equal Scaling Law: For optimal training compute efficiency, model size (NNN) and training data (DDD) must scale at equal rates (1:1). If you double the compute budget, you should double both the parameter count and the number of tokens. Analytics Vidhya The ~20:1 Golden Ratio: A model trained to compute-optimal efficiency requires roughly 20 tokens per parameter (D≈20ND \approx 20ND≈20N). Analytics Vidhya Massive LLMs were severely undertrained: Most high-profile LLMs built between 2020 and 2022 (e.g., GPT-3, Gopher, Megatron-Turing NLG) were far too large relative to the amount of data they were trained on. Michael Brenndoerfer Proof with Chinchilla (70B): DeepMind built Chinchilla, a 70B parameter model trained on 1.4 trillion tokens. Despite having 2.5×2.5\times2.5× fewer parameters than GPT-3 (175B) and Gopher (280B), Chinchilla outperformed both models across virtually every benchmark while using substantially less training compute. Analytics Vidhya Mathematical Loss Equation: They formalized the loss function incorporating an irreducible loss (EEE): L(N,D)=E+ANα+BDβ L(N, D) = E + \frac{A}{N^\alpha} + \frac{B}{D^\beta} L(N,D)=E+NαA​+DβB​ where optimal parameters scale as Nopt∝CaN_{opt} \propto C^aNopt​∝Ca and Dopt∝CbD_{opt} \propto C^bDopt​∝Cb, finding a≈0.5a \approx 0.5a≈0.5 and b≈0.5b \approx 0.5b≈0.5.
data.legacy--post-chinchilla-era#Legacy \u002: Inference-Optimal Over-training: While Chinchilla defined compute-optimal training, modern open-weights models (like Llama 3 8B trained on 15T+ tokens—a 1,800:1 ratio) intentionally break Chinchilla laws. They pay a higher training cost upfront to get a smaller model that is substantially cheaper and faster to run at inference across millions of user

LLM training optimization spans distributed parallelization, memory management, kernel-level execution, numerical precision, and algorithmic architecture.
Medium
Tensor Parallelism (TP): Splits individual matrix multiplications across GPUs within a single node (e.g., Megatron-LM splitting MLP and Attention weight matrices column-wise and row-wise). Requires low-latency interconnects (NVLink). Pipeline Parallelism (PP): Partitions layers sequentially across multiple nodes (e.g., GPipe, Megatron-LM 1F1B schedule). Uses micro-batching to reduce pipeline bubbles. Context Parallelism (CP / RingAttention): Shards the sequence dimension across devices to process ultra-long contexts (64k+64\text{k}+64k+ to 1M+1\text{M}+1M+ tokens) without exhausting single-device memory. Expert Parallelism (EP): For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, routes token embeddings dynamically to specialized feed-forward experts partitioned across different ranks via All-to-All communication. 3D/4D Parallelism: Combines DP, TP, PP, and CP to scale training across tens of thousands of GPUs.
data.2-memory-reduction--sharding#2. Memory R: ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) / FSDP: Stage 1: Shards optimizer states across data-parallel ranks (saves ≈4×\approx 4\times≈4× memory). Stage 2: Shards optimizer states and gradients (saves ≈8×\approx 8\times≈8× memory). Stage 3 / Full FSDP: Shards optimizer states, gradients, and model parameters. Dynamically gathers parameters on-demand during forward/backward passes and discards them immediately. Activation / Gradient Checkpointing: Discards intermediate forward-pass activations and recomputes them during the backward pass, trading ∼20–30%\sim 20\text{–}30\%∼20–30% compute overhead for drastic activation memory reduction. Selective Activation Recomputation: Recomputes only memory-heavy, compute-cheap operations (such as attention score softmax/dropout) while caching compute-heavy GEMM activations. CPU / NVMe Offloading (ZeRO-Offload): Offloads optimizer states and infrequently accessed weights from high-bandwidth HBM to host memory during step updates.
data.3-kernel--compute-acceleration#3. Kernel: FlashAttention (v1, v2, v3): IO-aware tiling algorithms that compute exact scaled dot-product attention in fast on-chip SRAM. Avoids materializing the O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) attention matrix in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), drastically cutting memory bandwidth bottlenecks. Operator Fusion: Merges adjacent pointwise, normalization, and linear operations (e.g., RMSNorm + GEMM, SwiGLU, fused AdamW) to eliminate redundant kernel launches and intermediate global-memory round-trips. Deep Learning Compilers: Frameworks like PyTorch Dynamo/torch.compile, Triton, and XLA generate optimized, hardware-specific C++/CUDA kernels with automatic layout transformations and graph fusions. Communication Overlap: Hides collective communication overhead (AllReduce, ReduceScatter, AllGather) behind independent compute kernels using CUDA streams and double-buffering.
data.4-precision--numerical-formats#4. Precis: Mixed Precision (AMP with BF16 / FP16): Stores weights, activations, and gradients in 16-bit while tracking optimizer states and weight master copies in FP32. BF16 is preferred over FP16 due to its dynamic range matching FP32, eliminating manual loss scaling. FP8 Training: Utilizes E4M3 (forward activations/weights) and E5M2 (backward gradients) formats supported on newer accelerator architectures (Hopper, Blackwell) to halve HBM footprints and double Tensor Core throughput. Stochastic Rounding: Mitigates gradient underflow and quantization error when accumulating low-bit gradient updates into low-precision master weights.
data.5-architectural--algorithmic-optimizatio: Attention Variants: Multi-Query Attention (MQA) & Grouped-Query Attention (GQA): Shares key/value projections across heads, decreasing memory traffic and cache footprint during autoregressive rollout and training. Sliding Window / Local Attention: Restricts attention computation to a localized context window. Optimizers: Memory-Efficient Optimizers: Adafactor, Lion, and 8-bit Adam (bitsandbytes) compress or factorize optimizer second-moment accumulators from 8 bytes/param down to 1–2 bytes/param. Muon / Shampoo: Second-order or orthogonalized momentum optimizers that accelerate convergence per token compared to standard AdamW. Data Packing: Concatenates multiple short token sequences into a single fixed-length window separated by attention masks to eliminate padding-token compute waste. Curriculum & Variable-Length Batching: Schedules sequence lengths progressively (e.g., training on 2k2\text{k}2k tokens before expanding to 8k+8\text{k}\text{+}8k+) to minimize compute early in training.
data.6-parameter-efficient-fine-tuning-peft#6:
When adapting pre-trained models rather than pretraining from scratch:
Method Mechanism Parameter Footprint LoRA / QLoRA Injects low-rank decomposition matrices (W0+BAW_0+BAW0​+BA) into attention/MLP layers; QLoRA quantizes the base model to 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4). ≪1%\ll 1\%≪1% trainable params DoRA Decomposes weight matrices into magnitude and directional components, applying LoRA solely to the direction vector. ≪1%\ll 1\%≪1% trainable params Prefix Tuning / Prompt Tuning Prepends trainable continuous virtual tokens to key/value or input embeddings. <0.1%<0.1\%<0.1% trainable params

Context Parallelism (CP)—often referred to as Sequence Parallelism across nodes, or realized via primitives like RingAttention and DeepSpeed-Ulysses—is an intra-layer distributed training and inference paradigm that partitions the sequence (context) dimension SSS across PPP accelerators while leaving the model’s weight matrices intact on each rank.
Where Tensor Parallelism (TP) splits the hidden dimension hhh (or attention heads hheadsh_{\text{heads}}hheads​) and hits an intra-node barrier (P≤8P \le 8P≤8), Context Parallelism enables scaling sequence lengths to hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens (S≥1MS \ge 1\text{M}S≥1M) across multi-node clusters by distributing activation memory and compute quadratically tied to sequence length.
In standard Transformer architectures, self-attention memory and compute scale with sequence length SSS:
Compute (FLOPs): O(S2⋅d)\mathcal{O}(S^2 \cdot d)O(S2⋅d) per head. Activation Memory: Attention logits require O(B⋅h⋅S2)\mathcal{O}(B \cdot h \cdot S^2)O(B⋅h⋅S2) in vanilla attention, or O(B⋅h⋅S⋅d)\mathcal{O}(B \cdot h \cdot S \cdot d)O(B⋅h⋅S⋅d) under online Softmax engines like FlashAttention. KV Cache (Inference): Scales linearly with SSS per request: 2×2×B×S×L×hKV×dk2 \times 2 \times B \times S \times L \times h_{KV} \times d_k2×2×B×S×L×hKV​×dk​ bytes. When scaling S→128kS \to 128\text{k}S→128k or 1M1\text{M}1M, a single GPU’s High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) is overwhelmed by activations even if the model weights fit completely. TP cannot shard SSS inside the core attention computation without cross-head communication, and Pipeline Parallelism (PP) requires activations of the entire sequence to be buffered between stage handoffs. Context Parallelism directly addresses this by slicing inputs:
X∈RB×S×d ⟹ X(p)∈RB×SP×d,p∈{0,1,…,P−1} X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times S \times d} \implies X^{(p)} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times \frac{S}{P} \times d}, \quad p \in \{0, 1, \dots, P-1\} X∈RB×S×d⟹X(p)∈RB×PS​×d,p∈{0,1,…,P−1} Each rank holds a sub-sequence of length s=S/Ps = S/Ps=S/P.
data.2-the-core-challenge-cross-rank-attentio:
Feedforward networks (MLPs), RMSNorm/LayerNorm, and embedding lookups operate element-wise or across token features independently. Sharding along SSS means these layers run locally on rank ppp with zero cross-rank communication:
HMLP(p)=MLP(X(p)) H_{\text{MLP}}^{(p)} = \text{MLP}\left(X^{(p)}\right) HMLP(p)​=MLP(X(p)) The fundamental challenge arises strictly at Self-Attention: token iii on rank ppp must attend to all tokens j≤ij \le ij≤i (under causal masking) or all tokens j∈[0,S−1]j \in [0, S-1]j∈[0,S−1] (under bidirectional attention), many of which reside in the memory of ranks q≠pq \ne pq=p.
Two primary architectures have emerged to solve this: RingAttention and DeepSpeed-Ulysses.
data.3-paradigm-a-ringattention-p2p-overlappe: Proposed by Hao Liu et al., RingAttention distributes the query, key, and value sequences across a logical ring of PPP GPUs.
data.4-causal-masking-imbalance-and-striped-r:
In causal auto-regressive models, token iii can only attend to token jjj where j≤ij \le ij≤i.
If sequences are sliced contiguously into linear chunks:
GPU 0 gets tokens [0,SP−1][0, \frac{S}{P}-1][0,PS​−1]: It only computes self-attention on its own tokens; all subsequent ring chunks from GPUs 1…P−11 \dots P-11…P−1 are masked out (0%0\%0% compute on those steps). GPU P−1P-1P−1 gets tokens [(P−1)SP,S−1][\frac{(P-1)S}{P}, S-1][P(P−1)S​,S−1]: It must attend to all past tokens (100%100\%100% compute across all PPP steps). This creates an extreme compute imbalance where GPU 0 sits idle while GPU P−1P-1P−1 bottlenecks the cluster, yielding ~50% hardware underutilization.
Naive Block Assignment: GPU 0: [■ □ □ □] -> 25% compute GPU 1: [■ ■ □ □] -> 50% compute GPU 2: [■ ■ ■ □] -> 75% compute GPU 3: [■ ■ ■ ■] -> 100% compute (Bottleneck)
data.5-paradigm-b-deepspeed-ulysses-all-to-al:
While RingAttention uses circular asynchronous P2P, DeepSpeed-Ulysses leverages global All-to-All collective communication primitives to swap between sequence partitioning and attention-head partitioning.
Input: Slices along Sequence [S/P, H] │ ▼ [ All-to-All-v Collective ] <-- Transposes (S/P, H) -> (S, H/P) │ ▼ Compute Attention locally on [S, H/P] via FlashAttention (Full Sequence, Subset of Heads) │ ▼ [ All-to-All-v Collective ] <-- Transposes (S, H/P) -> (S/P, H) │ ▼ Output: Slices along Sequence [S/P, H] Before Attention: Activations are partitioned along sequence length SP\frac{S}{P}PS​, holding all heads HHH. First All-to-All: Ranks exchange slices so each GPU now holds the entire sequence length SSS, but only a subset of heads HP\frac{H}{P}PH​. Local Compute: Standard optimized FlashAttention runs locally on full context SSS for HP\frac{H}{P}PH​ heads with zero custom communication or online softmax stitching. Second All-to-All: The attention output tensor is transposed back from [S,HP][S, \frac{H}{P}][S,PH​] to [SP,H][\frac{S}{P}, H][PS​,H] to resume element-wise MLP computation.

In large-scale production training (e.g., Llama 3, DeepSeek-V3), Context Parallelism forms a dedicated dimension in the parallel process grid:
World Size=TP×PP×DP (FSDP)×CP 	ext{World Size} = 	ext{TP} 	imes 	ext{PP} 	imes 	ext{DP (FSDP)} 	imes 	ext{CP} World Size=TP×PP×DP (FSDP)×CP Intra-node: Tensor Parallelism (TP ≤8\le 8≤8) operates within a single NVLink domain due to sub-microsecond latency demands. data:
Tensor Parallelism (TP) is an intra-layer model-parallelism technique that splits individual weight matrices, matrix multiplications (GEMMs), and activations across multiple accelerators (GPUs/TPUs).
Unlike Pipeline Parallelism (PP)—which partitions models across sequential layers and introduces execution bubbles—or Data Parallelism (DP/FSDP)—which replicates model weights or shards parameters across batch dimensions—Tensor Parallelism splits individual weight tensors within a layer to compute a single layer cooperatively across multiple ranks.
data.1-mathematical-foundations-1d-matrix-par:
Consider a standard fully connected layer computing Y=Activation(XW)Y = \text{Activation}(XW)Y=Activation(XW), where:
Input activation X∈RB×dinX \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times d_{in}}X∈RB×din​ (batch size B×B \timesB× sequence length SSS, flattened to dimension BBB) Weight matrix W∈Rdin×doutW \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{in} \times d_{out}}W∈Rdin​×dout​ Output activation Y∈RB×doutY \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times d_{out}}Y∈RB×dout​ Across NNN parallel processing ranks, a matrix multiplication can be sliced along its columns or its rows.
Naively chaining parallel layers requires an All-Gather after each column-parallel layer and an All-Reduce after each row-parallel layer, creating substantial collective communication overhead.
The core insight of Megatron-LM is pairing Column-Parallel and Row-Parallel layers back-to-back to cancel intermediate communications.
MLP Forward Pass: X (Replicated) │ ├──► GPU 0: [W1_col] ──► GeLU ──► [W2_row] ──┐ │ │ (All-Reduce Sum) └──► GPU 1: [W2_col] ──► GeLU ──► [W2_row] ──┴──► Output (Replicated)

data.4-communication-overhead-and-topology-co:
A standard Ring All-Reduce transfers 2⋅N−1N⋅S2 \cdot \frac{N-1}{N} \cdot S2⋅NN−1​⋅S bytes for a tensor of size SSS.
For a Transformer layer with sequence length LLL, batch size BBB, and hidden dimension hhh:
The tensor transmitted in each All-Reduce is activation Y∈RB×L×hY \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times L \times h}Y∈RB×L×h. In 16-bit precision (FP16/BF16), total bytes per All-Reduce: Bytes=2×B×L×h×2=4BLh \text{Bytes} = 2 \times B \times L \times h \times 2 = 4BLh Bytes=2×B×L×h×2=4BLh Total forward communication per layer: VolumeFWD=2×2(N−1N)(2BLh)=8BLh(N−1N) bytes \text{Volume}_{\text{FWD}} = 2 \times 2 \left(\frac{N-1}{N}\right) (2BLh) = 8BLh \left(\frac{N-1}{N}\right) \text{ bytes} VolumeFWD​=2×2(NN−1​)(2BLh)=8BLh(NN−1​) bytes Because this communication happens on every single Transformer layer in the critical path (blocking further GEMM computation), Tensor Parallelism has strict latency requirements:
Bandwidth bottleneck: Inter-node networking (e.g., 400 Gbps / 50 GB/s HDR/NDR InfiniBand) introduces high latency stalls relative to kernel execution times. Hardware constraint: Tensor Parallelism is almost exclusively restricted to intra-node domains linked via high-speed interconnects (NVLink / NVSwitch at 900 GB/s to 1.8 TB/s per GPU). TP degree is typically set to N≤8N \le 8N≤8 (matching single-node GPU density).
data.5-evolution-sequence-parallelism-megatro:
In vanilla 1D TP, the operations outside the Attention and MLP blocks—specifically LayerNorm and Dropout—are replicated identically across all NNN ranks:
Vanilla TP: Input ──► [LayerNorm (Replicated)] ──► [Col-GEMM] ──► ... ──► [Row-GEMM] ──► [All-Reduce] ──► [Dropout] This causes two problems:
Redundant compute for LayerNorm/Dropout. Activation memory for LayerNorm inputs/outputs cannot be sharded, dominating memory consumption at long contexts (L≥8kL \ge 8\text{k}L≥8k). Sequence Parallelism (SP) solves this by observing that the All-Reduce operation in Row-Parallel linear layers is decomposed into:
All-Reduce=Reduce-Scatter+All-Gather \text{All-Reduce} = \text{Reduce-Scatter} + \text{All-Gather} All-Reduce=Reduce-Scatter+All-Gather Instead of running an All-Reduce at the end of the row-parallel projection, Megatron-SP runs a Reduce-Scatter:
The partial sums are reduced and simultaneously scattered along the sequence dimension (L/NL/NL/N). LayerNorm and Dropout execute on local slices of sequence length LN\frac{L}{N}NL​ with zero communication. Before the next Column-Parallel projection, an All-Gather reassembles the full sequence across all ranks. Megatron-SP: [Row-GEMM] ──► [Reduce-Scatter along S] ──► [LayerNorm on S/N] ──► [Dropout on S/N] ──► [All-Gather along S] ──► [Col-GEMM] Communication volume remains identical to vanilla 1D TP (since Cost(Reduce-Scatter)+Cost(All-Gather)=Cost(All-Reduce)\text{Cost}(\text{Reduce-Scatter}) + \text{Cost}(\text{All-Gather}) = \text{Cost}(\text{All-Reduce})Cost(Reduce-Scatter)+Cost(All-Gather)=Cost(All-Reduce)), but activation memory from LayerNorm and Dropout drops by a factor of NNN.

data.a-full-activation-checkpointing-remateri:
Mechanism: Discards all intermediate activations inside each transformer block after the forward pass, retaining only the single input tensor entering each layer (b×s×hb \times s \times hb×s×h).
During Backward: Re-executes the forward pass for that block on-the-fly to regenerate the necessary activations.
Trade-off: Adds ~30–33% compute overhead (one extra forward pass), but reduces activation memory from O(L⋅s2)O(L \cdot s^2)O(L⋅s2) down to roughly:
Mact≈2⋅b⋅s⋅L⋅h bytesM_{\text{act}} \approx 2 \cdot b \cdot s \cdot L \cdot h \text{ bytes}Mact​≈2⋅b⋅s⋅L⋅h bytes
data.b-flashattention-tiling--online-softmax#:
Mechanism: Fuses the attention calculation into a single GPU SRAM kernel using online softmax. It never writes the large b×a×s×sb \times a \times s \times sb×a×s×s attention matrix to high-bandwidth memory (HBM).
Impact: Eliminates the quadratic O(s2)O(s^2)O(s2) memory term entirely, making attention memory scale strictly linear with sequence length sss.

data:
Zero Redundancy Optimizer (ZeRO) and Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP) are memory optimization techniques that scale Data Parallelism by slicing a model’s memory footprint across multiple GPUs, enabling the training of models far larger than a single GPU’s VRAM limits.
Memory reduction across ZeRO Stages. Source: Medium
ZeRO Stage 1 (Optimizer State Partitioning) In standard data parallelism, every GPU holds a full copy of the optimizer states (like Adam’s momentum and variance), consuming massive memory. Stage 1 partitions these states across the cluster. Each GPU holds and updates only its assigned slice of the optimizer state.
ZeRO Stage 2 (Gradient Partitioning) Builds on Stage 1 by also partitioning the gradients. During the backward pass, a GPU computes gradients and retains only the specific slice it is responsible for updating, immediately discarding the rest to free memory.
ZeRO Stage 3 (Parameter Partitioning) The most aggressive form of ZeRO, dividing the actual model weights across all GPUs. No single GPU holds the full model. During forward and backward passes, a GPU dynamically fetches the required parameter slices from other GPUs using an All-Gather operation, computes the layer, and instantly discards the fetched weights.
ZeRO-Offload and ZeRO-Infinity Extensions of the ZeRO architecture that move optimizer states, gradients, or parameters out of GPU VRAM and onto CPU RAM or NVMe storage. This trades communication speed for massive capacity, allowing trillion-parameter model training on limited hardware.
Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP) FSDP is PyTorch’s native, highly optimized implementation of ZeRO Stage 3. It shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across data-parallel workers. FSDP wraps individual layers (like transformer blocks) and automatically manages the complex All-Gather (fetching weights before computation) and Reduce-Scatter (synchronizing gradients after computation) operations under the hood, making it the standard choice for modern PyTorch-based LLM training.
Recurrent architectures process sequential data by maintaining an internal hidden state that persists information across time steps.

At each time step ttt, it updates its hidden state ht\mathbf{h}_tht​ based on the current input xt\mathbf{x}_txt​ and the previous hidden state ht−1\mathbf{h}_{t-1}ht−1​.
